solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Successful entertainer bursts out with energy in rush

indicators.note: 'out with energy' asks for the energy symbol to be thrown out of the word for rush

blocks.note: a balloon pops when it bursts
to tear is to rush; take out E for energy

explanation.surface: A performer erupts onto the stage in a burst of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bursts out' looks like a single phrase, but 'out' belongs with 'energy': TEAR, to rush, with its E put out.
explanation.definitionFit: A pop star is a performer of popular music, and one with hits counts as a success.

clue.text: Immature creature raised in a year

indicators.note: the word for raised sits in the abbreviation for a year

blocks.note: per annum, Latin for a year, abbreviated
something raised is up

explanation.surface: A young animal reared over the course of twelve months.
explanation.walkthrough: PA is p.a., per annum, as in a salary quoted per year.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupa is the insect stage between larva and adult, so it is an undeveloped form of the creature.

clue.text: One in favour of street rioting?

definitions.text: One in favour of street rioting?

indicators.note: letters that riot run wild and lose their order

blocks.note: a pro is someone for something
the six letters of street rearranged

explanation.surface: A description of someone who is all for violence in the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and, read as a question, a picture of the answer: someone backing a street riot.
explanation.definitionFit: A protester takes to the streets, and demonstrations sometimes turn into riots, so the whole description fits.

clue.text: Story in the Mirror?

blocks.note: the surface reads as a report printed in the Mirror, a British tabloid newspaper
the setter means a tale set inside a looking-glass: Lewis Carroll's sequel in which Alice climbs through one

explanation.surface: A news item carried by the Daily Mirror tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M sends you to the newspaper; the story is Lewis Carroll's 1871 sequel to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, where Alice steps into the world behind a mirror.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's book is a story whose whole world lies inside a mirror, a looking-glass.

clue.text: Deer’s round bottom, reddish

indicators.note: the deer goes round the word for bottom, holding it inside

blocks.note: a roe is a small deer
your seat is what you sit on

explanation.surface: A description of a deer's rump as being ruddy in colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is': the deer is round the bottom. It is easy to read it as a possessive and look for a part of a deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Roseate means rose-coloured, a pinkish shade of red.

clue.text: Novel about Churchill’s bunker?

blocks.note: Anthony Trollope's first Barsetshire novel, published in 1855
Churchill ran the Second World War from the underground Cabinet War Rooms; split the title three ways to describe them

explanation.surface: A work of fiction set around Winston Churchill's wartime underground headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the title three ways, THE WAR DEN, and it describes the Cabinet War Rooms beneath Whitehall; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's The Warden is a Victorian novel about a clergyman in charge of an almshouse.

clue.text: What master mason has leads to serious questioning

blocks.note: in Freemasonry, master mason is the rank of the highest of the three craft grades
the idiom for a gruelling interrogation

explanation.surface: A senior Freemason's status brings him intense interrogation.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a noun phrase naming a rank, while the second describes an ordeal; the same words cover both.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the third degree means harsh, lengthy interrogation, and Freemasons rise through three degrees to become master masons.

clue.text: Besotted with slinky demeanour

indicators.note: slinky describes a sinuous, sliding movement, so the letters slide about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone is smitten by another person's sinuous, seductive bearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' can look like part of the definition; it just joins, as the letters come from demeanour alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To be besotted is to be infatuated, head over heels in love.

clue.text: Drink at pub for leading character

blocks.note: ale is beer
PH, public house, as on Ordnance Survey maps

explanation.surface: Someone orders a drink at the pub for the main person in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' simply puts the drink next to the pub; PH is the standard abbreviation for a public house.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, so it leads all the other characters.

clue.text: Go off outside, denied kiss during tryst

indicators.note: the word for outside is refused the kiss, so that letter is taken away
what happens during something sits in its middle

blocks.note: a tryst is a romantic date
exterior means outside; remove X, the kiss

explanation.surface: A lover storms off outdoors after being refused a kiss on a date.
explanation.walkthrough: X for a kiss is the sign at the end of a letter. 'Go off' reads as leaving; it means spoil.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that goes off spoils, becoming worse, which is what deteriorate means.

clue.text: A need for baby, so sleep with cousin

blocks.note: a nap is a short sleep
a cousin is one of your kin, your relatives

explanation.surface: A baby needs a rest, so it naps alongside a young relative.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the formal British word for a nappy, which is what a baby needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Napkin is the full, old-fashioned form of nappy, a diaper, something every baby requires.

clue.text: House warming’s ending with a fine foxtrot

indicators.note: the ending of the word warming is its final letter

blocks.note: the last letter of warming
used as it is
F for fine, as on pencils
Foxtrot is F in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A housewarming party finishes with a graceful ballroom dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House warming' reads as one idea, a party, but 'House' is the definition and 'warming' supplies only its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaff is British slang for a home, where someone lives.

clue.text: Good to move down exhibition hall showing sensitivity

indicators.note: in a down answer the letter for good is shifted lower down the hall, lodging near the bottom

blocks.note: G is the usual abbreviation for good
a gallery, with its first letter taken away to be moved

explanation.surface: Visitors are asked to proceed down a gallery while showing tact.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the G from the front of GALLERY and slide it further down the word, to just before the Y.
explanation.definitionFit: An allergy is a physical oversensitivity to a substance such as pollen.

clue.text: Police perhaps paid to break hunger strike?

blocks.note: a police force; 'perhaps' because it is one example
read as FEE'D: given a fee

explanation.surface: Officers were bribed to end a prisoner's fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paid' is a jokey coinage, fee'd; the question mark owns up to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunger strikers such as the suffragettes were force-fed to end their refusal to eat.

clue.text: Having run down, rare warmth envelops players

indicators.note: letters that have run have streamed away from their places, as dye runs in the wash

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 22 letters

explanation.surface: Someone worn out wraps themselves in unusual warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run down' reads as tired, but 'down' is fodder and 'Having run' the signal; one word, 'players', defines 22 letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolverhampton Wanderers, known as Wolves, is an English professional football club, a team of players.

clue.text: Put off edited satanic report

indicators.note: an edited text has been rearranged and reworked

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: Readers are repelled by a doctored account of devil worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put off' reads as disgusted; it means delay.
explanation.definitionFit: To procrastinate is to delay or postpone doing something, to keep putting it off.

clue.text: Two toys are nearly maximum price

indicators.note: two toys means a pair of separate toy words set side by side
nearly means almost all, so the final letter is not reached

blocks.note: a spinning top, the first toy
a doll, the second toy
the verb 'are' without its last letter

explanation.surface: A pair of playthings cost almost the most anyone could charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two toys' asks for two different toys, one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying top dollar is an idiom for paying the highest price.

clue.text: Outfit with green energy

blocks.note: a getup is an outfit of clothes
with and 'and' both join
green at a traffic light means go

explanation.surface: Clothing made with environmentally sound power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green energy' reads as renewable power, but 'energy' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Get-up-and-go is informal for drive and enthusiasm, personal vigour.

clue.text: No time for sexy poetry after hard alexandrines

indicators.note: with no room for time, its abbreviation is struck out
the poetry comes after the word for hard, so it is placed second

blocks.note: H for hard, as on pencils
erotic verse loses T, the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A prudish reader has no patience with racy poems after struggling with a difficult metre.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads backwards: hard comes first, then the poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandrines, twelve-syllable lines, are the classical metre of French epic and tragedy, the heroic verse of that language.

clue.text: Wife aggressively masculine, daughter not born

indicators.note: daughter comes in and born does not, so one letter takes the other's place

blocks.note: butch means ostentatiously tough and manly
D for daughter, from genealogy
B for born, the letter that is swapped out

explanation.surface: A wife who is aggressively manly and has no daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My old Dutch' is Cockney for one's wife, from rhyming slang Duchess of Fife.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney slang a man's wife is his old Dutch, a crossword-friendly sense of the word.

clue.text: Start to type one’s newspaper article up, to put by for later

indicators.note: 'start to type' is the first letter of type, the opening piece
in a down answer, up means the pieces are read from the bottom

blocks.note: first letter of type
one is I; with 's, IS
an op-ed is a comment piece opposite the editorial page

explanation.surface: A journalist starts typing up their piece to save it for later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reads as typing up; in a down clue it reverses everything before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To deposit money is to put it by, lodging it in a bank for later use.

clue.text: Hatred of how much senior management take

blocks.note: an exec is an executive
a ration is how much each person may take
surface padding that completes the phrase 'how much ... take', the share allotted

explanation.surface: Resentment of the amount top bosses pay themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads as a phrase, exec ration, the share executives take: the surface grievance is the answer split in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Execration is loathing, the act of cursing or denouncing someone bitterly.

clue.text: So much French booze leads to furious scene

blocks.note: tant is French for so much
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: Too much drinking in France ends in an angry row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' modifies 'so much', not 'booze': translate the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A tantrum is an outburst of rage, making an angry scene.

clue.text: Sea wall gone extremely rapidly in a storm

indicators.note: the extremes of rapidly are its outermost letters
things caught in a storm are tossed about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, as printed
first and last letters of rapidly

explanation.surface: A sea wall collapses very quickly in bad weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' reads as intensifying 'rapidly'; it takes its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A groyne is a low wall built out from a beach into the sea to check erosion.

clue.text: Around part of eye, note the foreign pattern of stitches

indicators.note: the note and the foreign word go around the part of the eye

blocks.note: fa, the fourth note of the sol-fa scale
le is French for the
the coloured ring of the eye

explanation.surface: An instruction about the pattern of stitches round an eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stitches' suggests surgery on the eye; it is knitting. The two outer pieces wrap the eye part, the second being French.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair Isle is a style of multicoloured knitting from the Shetland island of that name.

clue.text: Chief steward brought round tea for customer

indicators.note: the steward is brought round the tea, wrapping it

blocks.note: the purser is the senior steward on a ship
cha, or char, is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: A head steward serves tea to a passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought round' reads as served; it wraps PURSER round the tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A purchaser is a buyer, and a customer is someone who buys.

clue.text: Arrange fielding position for critical moment of match

blocks.note: to set is to arrange
point is a cricket fielding position square of the batsman on the off side

explanation.surface: A cricket captain positions a fielder for the decisive stage of the game.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket; the answer is tennis. Point is a fielding position square of the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, set point is when one more point won settles a set, a crucial moment of the match.

clue.text: Girl half rejecting modern times

indicators.note: half means keep only one of the two halves of the phrase
to reject something is to throw it back

blocks.note: Anno Domini, the Christian era, cut to its first half

explanation.surface: A girl who is half inclined to spurn the present day.
explanation.walkthrough: Anno Domini, AD, marks the years of the modern era; its ten letters halve to ANNOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Donna is a girl's name, and in Italian simply means woman or lady.

clue.text: Piled up, a sea enveloping a ship

indicators.note: the sea wraps around the second 'a' and ship

blocks.note: used as it is
the Med, the Mediterranean Sea
A plus SS, steamship

explanation.surface: A ship is swamped and heaped up by the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two a's; the first stands alone and the second goes inside the Med with the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Amassed means gathered together in a large quantity, heaped or piled up.

clue.text: One bowing to audience in Buddhist shrine

indicators.note: what is said to an audience is heard, not read

blocks.note: one who stoops bows the head or back

explanation.surface: A worshipper bows before the congregation in a Buddhist temple.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent stooper and the shrine's name sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupa is a dome-shaped Buddhist monument housing relics, used as a place of worship.

clue.text: What some loose women had on highly embarrassed landlord?

definitions.text: What some loose women had on

blocks.note: someone deeply embarrassed goes scarlet
a landlord lets property, so is a letter

explanation.surface: A salacious remark about women who had a very embarrassed landlord in their grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had on' is both worn and teased; the question mark flags landlord as one who lets. Hawthorne's novel has Hester Prynne wear a red A for adultery.
explanation.definitionFit: Puritan adulteresses were made to wear a scarlet letter A as a public badge of shame.

clue.text: Chinese perhaps like Scotsman?

blocks.note: as and like both compare
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a Chinese person resembles a Scot.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that Ian stands for any Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: China is in Asia, so a Chinese person is an example of an Asian.

clue.text: Alarms heard when no poisonous gas remains in cans

indicators.note: to remain in something is to stay inside it

blocks.note: tins are cans
O looks like zero, none
CS gas is a tear gas

explanation.surface: Warnings sound when cans of poison gas are found to be empty.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface also plays on the answer sounding like toxins. CS gas is the riot-control agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Tocsins are alarm bells, rung as warnings, so they are alarms that are heard.

clue.text: Poet‘s good book very cheap?

blocks.note: Ezra is a book of the Old Testament, in the Good Book
something going for a pound is very cheap

explanation.surface: A writer's excellent volume is a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good book' reads as a fine read; the Good Book is the Bible, and Ezra is one of its books. A British pound shop sells everything for a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezra Pound was a major American modernist poet, author of The Cantos.

clue.text: Fought — as road was widened — to be heard?

indicators.note: what is heard is spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: a road widened into a dual carriageway has been dualled

explanation.surface: Two parties clashed noisily while a road was being widened.
explanation.walkthrough: A dual carriageway is the British term for a divided highway; widening a road to one is to dual it.
explanation.definitionFit: To duel is to fight formally, one against one, so duelled is fought.

clue.text: Flag officer goes by state during round of duty

indicators.note: what happens during something falls inside it

blocks.note: a tour of duty is a spell of service
RI, Rhode Island
Col., colonel

explanation.surface: An admiral travels through a country while on his rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag officer' reads as naval rank; 'Flag' is the definition and 'officer' starts the wordplay. 'goes by' sets COL beside the state.
explanation.definitionFit: A tricolour is a flag of three colour bands, such as the French or Irish flag.

clue.text: Judge vase one to discard, house being this?

blocks.note: a ref, referee, judges a game
an urn is a vase
I is one as a Roman numeral
to shed is to discard

explanation.surface: Someone assesses which vase to throw away while a house is being done up.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the wordplay: a house whose old items are shed and replaced is being given new contents.
explanation.definitionFit: A house being refurnished has its old furniture discarded and new pieces brought in.

clue.text: Sympathetic as firm friend admits strong agitation

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the friend takes the agitation inside

blocks.note: Co., company
a mate is a friend
passion is intense emotion

explanation.surface: A loyal friend is kind in confessing to deep distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm friend' reads as a close pal; 'firm' is a separate piece, the company.
explanation.definitionFit: Compassionate means feeling pity and concern for others, being sympathetic.

clue.text: Power to arouse emotion when one collapses fifty and active

indicators.note: a collapsed structure is left in a jumbled heap

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: It is moving when someone lively at fifty suddenly falls down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fifty' tempts you to write L; here it is fodder, spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: Affectivity is the capacity to stir the feelings, from affect, an emotional state.

clue.text: A number working across one’s back for stiffness

indicators.note: working goes across, past, the reversed piece, so it follows it
going back means reading the letters the other way

blocks.note: ten is a number
one is I, plus the 's
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Several men work across someone's back to ease stiffness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's back' reads as a body part, the obvious place for stiffness; it is wordplay, and 'stiffness' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Tension is tautness, as in muscles that are stiff and tight.

clue.text: Soprano suppresses a tear regularly, not beyond recovery

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, every other letter
to suppress is to hold down, keeping the rest inside

blocks.note: a treble is a boy soprano
used as it is
first and third letters of tear

explanation.surface: A singer holds back a tear now and then, still able to recover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soprano' tempts you to write S; the setter means a treble, the choirboy's voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treatable can be cured by medical care, so it is not past recovery.

clue.text: Affair takes one out of office work

indicators.note: taking one out removes the Roman numeral for one

blocks.note: filing, office work, minus I

explanation.surface: An office romance distracts someone from work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'office work' is filing; take out I, one.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both words name a short, casual romantic liaison, usually not meant to last.

clue.text: Obtained work on ship to produce magazine perhaps

blocks.note: got means obtained
op, opus, a work
re means on, concerning
SS, steamship

explanation.surface: Someone got work aboard a ship to publish a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The chunks cut across the word breaks: GOT OP RE SS regroups as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A publication goes to press when it is sent for printing, the final step in producing it.

clue.text: Think about where to move: coast

indicators.note: letters told to move change places
the verb for think goes about, around, the other letters

blocks.note: to feel is to think, as in 'I feel we should go'
the five letters of where rearranged

explanation.surface: A chess player considers their next move before taking things easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning'; it is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To freewheel is to coast along, as a cyclist does without pedalling.

clue.text: All energy, extremely desirable at first in youth

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter is used
the opening letter of desirable sits in the word for youth

blocks.note: E, energy
very means extremely
a boy is a youth
first letter of desirable

explanation.surface: A description of a young person who is full of energy and very attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All energy' reads as a description; 'All' is the definition and 'energy' just E.
explanation.definitionFit: Everybody means every person, all the people.

clue.text: Lock up enclosure ahead of time

blocks.note: enc., the abbreviation for enclosure on a letter
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Animals are shut in a pen before the time comes.
explanation.walkthrough: ENC. is the abbreviation printed at the foot of a letter to say something is enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: To encage is to shut in a cage, so to imprison or confine.

clue.text: Throw speaker’s aid into burner, causing scream?

indicators.note: throwing the aid into the burner lodges it inside
what is thrown into something ends up inside it

blocks.note: coal is burnt as fuel
a mic, microphone, helps a speaker be heard

explanation.surface: Someone hurls a microphone into a fire, making people shriek.
explanation.walkthrough: A scream is British informal for something hilarious; 'Throw' sets the scene and 'into' does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is a scream is very funny, so what causes one is comical.

clue.text: Piles on underclothes one may get down to

blocks.note: bras are underwear
stacks are piles

explanation.surface: Heaps of lingerie that someone might strip down to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts the piles after the underclothes. The definition plays on stripping down to underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: To get down to brass tacks is an idiom for turning to the essential practical details.

clue.text: To keep off alcohol, mostly locked away port

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter
the word for locked away is to keep the teetotal letters inside it

blocks.note: sealed, minus its last letter
TT, teetotal

explanation.surface: A drinker's alcohol is largely kept under lock and key to help them stay dry.
explanation.walkthrough: TT, teetotal, is the crossword standard for someone who does not drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Seattle is a major seaport on Puget Sound in Washington State.

clue.text: Very much gas around — died

indicators.note: turned around, the gas is read backwards

blocks.note: neon is a noble gas
D for died, in genealogy

explanation.surface: An awful lot of gas hung about and somebody died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' could be a container, but nothing goes inside: here it turns the gas round.
explanation.definitionFit: No end is an informal idiom for a great deal, as in 'it cheered her up no end'.

clue.text: Sorcerer initially hated terrible old curse

indicators.note: initially means taking the first letter
something terrible is in a dreadful state, disordered

blocks.note: first letter of sorcerer
the letters of hated rearranged

explanation.surface: A wizard is at first loathed for a dreadful ancient curse.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is short for 'God's death', a mild oath of Shakespeare's era.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Sdeath is an archaic exclamation, a minced oath used to swear in Elizabethan times.

clue.text: One will go for a spin, churning up terrible mud

definitions.text: One will go for a spin

indicators.note: churning stirs things so they mix and change order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A car goes for a drive, throwing up dreadful muck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go for a spin' reads as a drive in a car; the machine spins laundry dry.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumble drier dries clothes by spinning them round in a heated drum.

clue.text: Travelled over for round-up

blocks.note: rode means travelled on horseback
O, over, from cricket scoring

explanation.surface: Someone came riding in for a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: An over is six balls in cricket, written O on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: A rodeo was originally a round-up of cattle, before it meant the riding show.

clue.text: Soldier at attention; Marlowe, for example

blocks.note: a private is the lowest-ranked soldier
to have your eye on something is to be paying it attention

explanation.surface: A soldier stands to attention, a figure in a drill scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at attention' suggests drill; the setter means the eye, organ of watchful attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Marlowe, Raymond Chandler's hero, is a private detective, a private eye.

clue.text: Happy to wander round lake

indicators.note: the verb for wander goes round the lake's letter

blocks.note: to gad about is to wander
L, lake, as on maps

explanation.surface: Someone is pleased to stroll round a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' links; 'wander' is the verb gad.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both adjectives describe feeling pleased or delighted about something.

clue.text: Angry reaction engulfing small character

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up, holding inside

blocks.note: a backlash is a strong hostile reaction
S, small, as on clothes labels

explanation.surface: A furious response swallows up a minor personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small character' reads as a person of no importance; 'small' is S and 'character' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The backslash is a typographical character on a computer keyboard.

clue.text: Said to have gone out wearing fleece, unlikely to change?

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so only its sound counts

blocks.note: a person who has gone out, like a light, has died
in the wool: dressed in fleece

explanation.surface: A sheep that seemed to pass away while still in its coat.
explanation.walkthrough: Wool dyed before spinning holds its colour; the question mark flags the pun on a colour that will not change.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyed-in-the-wool means thoroughly ingrained, so a person of fixed views is unlikely to alter.

clue.text: Austen novel’s central characters take a step back for another woman

indicators.note: a step back in the alphabet swaps each middle letter for the one before it

blocks.note: Emma, Jane Austen's 1815 novel
the two middle letters, each one letter earlier in the alphabet

explanation.surface: The main figures in a Jane Austen book retreat in favour of a different heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' means letters: the middle pair of EMMA each move back one place in the alphabet, M becoming L.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is a woman's name, and Ella is a different woman's name.

clue.text: Frightfully secretive after short retreat

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its last letter

sly means secretive and cunning

explanation.surface: Someone is awfully furtive following a brief getaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts SLY after the curtailed hideout, reversing the clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Frightfully and hideously both mean in a horrible, dreadful way.

clue.text: Tried to get help after letter read out

indicators.note: reading something out makes it heard, so sound decides

blocks.note: ess is how the letter S is spoken, and aid is help

explanation.walkthrough: The letter is S, spoken as 'ess'; follow it with aid and say both.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay something is to attempt it, so essayed is a formal word for tried.
